intro: To use the Morph transition in PowerPoint on Mac, copy a slide, move or resize a few objects on the copy, then choose Morph on the Transitions tab. Morph then moves each matching object from the first slide to its new spot on the second, and Effect Options lets you pick Objects, Words, or Characters.
tldr: Copy your slide, then move, resize, or recolor a few objects on the copy.
Select the second slide, open the Transitions tab, and choose Morph.
Pick Objects, Words, or Characters in Effect Options. Objects suits most decks.
Morph needs PowerPoint for Microsoft 365 on Mac, version 15.19 or newer, and matching objects.
Test with ⌘⇧Return. Use the Selection Pane if Morph pairs the wrong objects.

blocks.text: What Morph does on a Mac
Morph is a slide transition. It takes the objects on one slide and moves each one into its matching object on the next slide. The result looks like one thing changing shape, not a plain fade.

Most people use Morph for a product photo that zooms in, a bullet list that turns into a diagram, or a logo that slides across the screen. The motion looks smooth because PowerPoint draws the frames between the two slides. You do not build those frames yourself.
Check your PowerPoint version before you start

Microsoft's training page says PowerPoint for Microsoft 365 on Mac needs version 15.19 or newer to create Morph. Check your version before you spend time on a deck. Microsoft's training page gives a File > Account check that is written for Windows, so look for the About item in the PowerPoint menu on your Mac.

The latest PowerPoint for Mac build in Microsoft's update history is 16.114.4 (build 26110224), released November 4, 2026. Microsoft's lifecycle page lists 16.83 as the minimum Mac app version that can update. If your version is older, update before you build anything important.

blocks.text: Office on a Mac also needs a supported macOS. Microsoft supports Office on the three most recent major versions of macOS. Starting July 13, 2026, Office apps on unsupported systems can open and print files but cannot edit, save, or create new files.

Two dates matter here. PowerPoint 2021 reached end of support on October 13, 2026. Office 2019 for Mac reached end of support on October 10, 2023. If you still run either one, plan an upgrade before your next big deck.
Set up two slides that share at least one object

Morph needs two slides that share at least one object. Microsoft's guidance is to copy a slide that has the objects you want to morph, then move those objects on the second slide. Start with the copy, not a blank slide.

items: Move a shape to a new spot on the slide.
Resize a picture or a text box.
Rotate an icon by a quarter turn.
Recolor a shape from one color to another.
Change a word in a title so Words mode has something to track.

blocks.text: If the second slide shares nothing with the first, Morph looks like a fade. Microsoft Support moderators make this point in their answers. Make at least one object clearly match, then test again.
Apply Morph and choose Objects, Words, or Characters

Click the second slide in the Thumbnail Pane on the left, so it is selected. Open the Transitions tab on the ribbon, then select Morph in the transition gallery. The transition belongs to the slide that comes in, so the second slide is the one to set.

Next, open Effect Options. You will see three choices. Objects moves whole shapes. Words moves text one word at a time. Characters moves letters one at a time. Each choice changes what PowerPoint treats as a match.

Objects is the right choice for most decks. Use it for pictures, icons, logos, and simple shapes. Use Words when a title changes from one slide to the next and you want each word to glide. Use Characters only for short text that should change one letter at a time. Characters can look busy, so test it at full speed.
Match shapes by name when Morph pairs the wrong objects

Morph pairs objects on its own, and sometimes it pairs the wrong ones. When that happens, name the objects yourself. Open Home > Arrange > Selection Pane, then rename each object you want to match. Give the matching object on the second slide the same name.

Start each name with two exclamation point characters, then a plain word such as Logo. Microsoft lists this naming scheme as supported on Mac from version 16.23. Each name must be unique on its slide. Morph does not pair a prefixed object with an unprefixed one, and it only pairs objects of the same type.
Check the result with a slide show

Microsoft's training page lists a Preview step after the Transitions settings. The Mac support page does not show where Preview sits on the ribbon, so look for it on the Transitions tab. If you cannot find it, skip straight to the slide show.

The slide show is the real test. Play the deck from the second slide and watch the motion at full speed. Repeat after each change, and do not trust a single run. If the motion looks off, go back to the matching step.
Keyboard shortcuts for testing a Morph deck
Microsoft's documentation does not list a Morph-specific shortcut. These shortcuts control the slide show, so you can test the motion fast.

items: ⌘⇧Return starts the slide show from the first slide.
⌘Return starts from the slide you are on.
Esc, the hyphen key, or ⌘. ends the show.
Press / during a show to open the shortcut list.

blocks.text: Microsoft's shortcut tables disagree on one line. One table maps start from current slide to ⌘⇧F5, while the delivery page gives ⌘Return. This guide uses ⌘Return. If it does nothing on your Mac, try ⌘⇧F5.
A worked example: a logo that glides into place

Say your first slide has a logo in the top left corner and a headline underneath. Copy the slide, so both slides have the logo and the headline. On the copy, drag the logo to the center and make it larger. Leave the headline where it is, so the eye has a fixed point.

Select the copy, choose Morph, and pick Objects. Then press ⌘⇧Return. The logo should glide to the center and grow while the headline stays put. If the logo jumps, check that both logos are the same type and that neither has a naming problem.
Common mistakes that make Morph look like a fade

items: Duplicating the slide and changing nothing, so nothing matches.
Moving an object that has no partner on the next slide.
Pairing a picture with a text box. Morph needs the same object type.
Using the same name twice on one slide.
Setting Morph on the first slide instead of the second.
Expecting a chart to morph. Charts cross-fade instead.

blocks.text: The partner mistake is the hardest to spot. A shape with no partner does not travel with the rest of the slide. Open the Selection Pane and check each object's name and type before you blame the transition.
Limits: shapes, charts, and sharing
PowerPoint cannot geometrically morph a custom shape with more than one hole. If you use a shape with a cutout, test it in the slide show. A simpler shape without the extra hole avoids the problem.

Charts do not morph. They cross-fade instead. Matched objects must also be the same type, so a table matches only a table, and SmartArt matches only SmartArt. Decide the type early, before you spend an afternoon on positions.

On the web, Morph works only for Microsoft 365 subscribers. The file must sit in OneDrive for work or school or in SharePoint, because Microsoft lists only those places. Test in the Mac app before you share a link.
Updates can move menus, and the history will not say why

Microsoft's update history lists versions, builds, and dates for PowerPoint for Mac. It does not describe changes, and no entry mentions Morph. If a menu moves after an update, the history will not explain it. Check the Transitions tab after each update, then run one test deck to be sure.
Where to go next

When Morph works, add a transition to the rest of the deck. Read [how to add a transition in PowerPoint on Mac](/how-to/add-a-transition-in-powerpoint) for the basic transitions. Then check [how to use Presenter View in PowerPoint on Mac](/how-to/use-presenter-view-in-powerpoint) before you present on a projector.

If the deck has to run on its own at a booth, read [how to loop a slide show in PowerPoint on Mac](/how-to/loop-a-slide-show-in-powerpoint). If you record narration over the animations, read [how to record a slide show in PowerPoint on Mac](/how-to/record-a-slide-show-in-powerpoint). Those guides use the same ribbon, so the menu names here will help.

faq.question: Do I need Microsoft 365 to use Morph on a Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft's training page says PowerPoint for Microsoft 365 on Mac, version 15.19 or newer, can create Morph. PowerPoint 2021 is also listed as able to create it. Check your version under the PowerPoint menu before you start.

faq.question: Why does my Morph transition look like a regular fade?
faq.answer: The two slides probably share nothing. Morph needs at least one object that matches on both slides. Duplicate the slide, change the copy, and play the show again. Microsoft Support suggests the same fix.

faq.question: Which version of PowerPoint for Mac is the latest?
faq.answer: Microsoft's update history lists 16.114.4 (build 26110224) as the latest PowerPoint for Mac build, released November 4, 2026. The page lists versions and dates only. It does not describe changes.

faq.question: Can I use Morph in PowerPoint for the web on a Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft says the web version works for Microsoft 365 subscribers with files stored in OneDrive for work or school or SharePoint. If your file lives somewhere else, use the Mac app.

faq.question: Does Morph work with charts?
faq.answer: No. Charts do not morph. PowerPoint cross-fades them instead. Build the part that must move from shapes if the motion matters.

faq.question: Why won't my shapes match even with the same name?
faq.answer: Check the type first. Morph matches only objects of the same type. Both objects also need the naming prefix, and each name must be unique on its slide. Microsoft lists this naming scheme from version 16.23 on Mac.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut for Morph itself?
faq.answer: Microsoft's documentation does not list one. Use ⌘⇧Return to start the slide show from the first slide, then check the motion.

faq.question: My Mac is old. Can I still edit Office files?
faq.answer: Microsoft supports Office on the three most recent major macOS versions. From July 13, 2026, Office apps on unsupported systems can open and print files but cannot edit, save, or create new files. Plan a macOS update or a newer Mac before you rely on Morph for a live deck.

faq.question: Does PowerPoint 2016 support Morph?
faq.answer: It can play Morph but cannot create it. Without the required Microsoft 365 updates, it plays a Fade transition instead.

task: Apply the Morph transition between two slides
appliesTo: PowerPoint for Microsoft 365 on Mac, version 15.19 or newer
requirements: PowerPoint for Microsoft 365 on Mac, version 15.19 or newer
Two slides in a row that share at least one object
Matching objects of the same type, named with the two exclamation point prefix if needed

steps.name: Open the deck and select your first slide
steps.text: Open the deck in PowerPoint for Mac. In the Thumbnail Pane on the left, click the first slide. This slide should already contain the objects you want to animate.
steps.tip: Morph only works between two slides that sit next to each other in the Thumbnail Pane.

steps.name: Duplicate the first slide
steps.text: Right-click the first slide in the Thumbnail Pane and choose Duplicate Slide. The copy appears right below the original. Leave the original as it is.
steps.tip: If you cannot find Duplicate Slide, select the slide, press ⌘C, then press ⌘V under the original.

steps.name: Change the objects on the copy
steps.text: Click the copy and move, resize, rotate, or recolor the objects you want to animate. A logo can move to a new corner. A picture can grow. A shape can change color.
steps.tip: Keep the other objects in place so the change you want stands out.

steps.name: Open the Transitions tab
steps.text: Click the copy in the Thumbnail Pane, then click the Transitions tab on the ribbon. The transition goes on the slide that comes in, which is the copy.

steps.name: Select Morph
steps.text: In the transition gallery, select Morph. PowerPoint applies it to the selected slide.

steps.name: Choose Objects, Words, or Characters
steps.text: Select Effect Options, then choose Objects. Use Words or Characters only when the text is the thing that changes.
steps.tip: Objects is the safe choice for most decks.

steps.name: Name matching objects if Morph guesses wrong
steps.text: Only do this when the result is wrong. Open the Selection Pane, then rename the matching objects on both slides with the same name. Start each name with two exclamation point characters, followed by a plain word such as Logo.
steps.tip: Each name must be unique on its slide, and both objects need the prefix.

steps.name: Run the slide show to test
steps.text: Press ⌘⇧Return to start from the first slide. Watch the second slide closely, then repeat after each change until the motion looks right.

troubleshooting.problem: Morph looks like a regular fade
troubleshooting.fix: Duplicate the slide, then move, resize, or recolor objects on the copy. Microsoft Support says a second slide with nothing in common looks like a fade.

troubleshooting.problem: Objects do not travel to their matches
troubleshooting.fix: Check that both objects are the same type and share a name with the two exclamation point prefix. Names must be unique on each slide. Edit names in Home > Arrange > Selection Pane.

troubleshooting.problem: Morph is missing from the transition gallery
troubleshooting.fix: Check your version. Microsoft's training page gives 15.19 or newer for Microsoft 365 on Mac. Update first, then look again on the Transitions tab.

troubleshooting.problem: A chart cross-fades instead of morphing
troubleshooting.fix: This is expected. Charts do not morph in PowerPoint. Rebuild the moving part from shapes, or accept the fade.

troubleshooting.problem: A custom shape will not morph geometrically
troubleshooting.fix: PowerPoint cannot geometrically morph a custom shape with more than one hole. Redraw the shape without the extra hole, or accept a simpler effect.
